Option A (70) is the total number who bring notebooks (20 + 50), which still includes the 20 who also bring course books, and option D mistakes the 30 course-books-only students for those who bring both.

questions.question: In a survey of a city, it was found that 65% of the people watched the news on television, 40% read a newspaper and 25% both read a newspaper and watched the news on television. What percentage of the people surveyed neither watched the news on television nor read a newspaper?
questions.explanation: The percentage who did at least one is 65% + 40% - 25% = 80%, since the 25% who did both are counted in both groups, so the percentage who did neither is 100% - 80% = 20%. Option D (80%) is the share who did at least one of the two, while options A (35%) and C (60%) remove only one group, giving those who did not watch the news and those who did not read a newspaper.

questions.question: Out of 400 students of a university, 102 studied Business Mathematics, 110 studied Management and 152 studied Business Law. Of these, 27 studied Management and Business Law, 36 studied Business Mathematics and Business Law, 18 studied Business Mathematics and Management, and 11 studied all three subjects. How many students did not study any of the three subjects?
questions.explanation: The number who studied at least one subject is 102 + 110 + 152 - 27 - 36 - 18 + 11 = 294, so 400 - 294 = 106 studied none. Option A (117) forgets to add back the 11 students taking all three subjects, option D (128) subtracts them instead, and option C (294) is the number who studied at least one subject.

questions.question: Out of 400 students of a university, 102 studied Business Mathematics, 110 studied Management and 152 studied Business Law. Of these, 27 studied Management and Business Law, 36 studied Business Mathematics and Business Law, 18 studied Business Mathematics and Management, and 11 studied all three subjects. How many students studied only one of the three subjects?
questions.explanation: Business Mathematics only = 102 - 36 - 18 + 11 = 59, Management only = 110 - 27 - 18 + 11 = 76 and Business Law only = 152 - 27 - 36 + 11 = 100, so 59 + 76 + 100 = 235 studied exactly one subject. Option C (202) forgets to add back the 11 all-three students in each 'only' count, option B (246) removes the 48 students taking exactly two subjects from 294 but forgets the 11 who took all three, and option A (294) counts everyone who studied at least one subject.

questions.question: A class of 60 students sat examinations in Mathematics, Statistics and Economics. 25 students failed Mathematics, 24 failed Statistics and 32 failed Economics. 9 failed Mathematics alone, 6 failed Statistics alone, 5 failed Statistics and Economics only, and 3 failed Mathematics and Statistics only. How many students failed all three subjects?
questions.explanation: Start with the Statistics circle, because all its other regions are known: 24 = 6 (Statistics alone) + 3 (Mathematics and Statistics only) + 5 (Statistics and Economics only) + x, so x = 10 failed all three. Option C comes from 25 - 9 - 3 = 13, which forgets the students who failed Mathematics and Economics only. Option A is the number who failed Economics alone (32 - 3 - 5 - 10 = 14), and option B is the number who failed at least one subject.

questions.question: Which of the following is an empty set?

options.b: {x : x is a state in Nigeria whose name begins with the letter L}
options.c: {x : x is an integer and 6 < x < 7}
options.d: {x : x is an integer and 6 < x < 8}

questions.explanation: There is no integer strictly between 6 and 7, so the set in option C has no element and is the empty set { }. Option A is not empty, because it contains one element, the number 0. Options D and B are singletons, {7} and {Lagos}.

questions.question: Which of the following is a singleton (unit) set?

options.a: {x : x is an integer and 4 < x < 5}
options.b: {x : x is an integer that is neither positive nor negative}
options.d: {x : x is a vowel in the word LAGOS}

questions.explanation: A singleton has exactly one element, and the only integer that is neither positive nor negative is 0, so option B is the set {0}. Option C is {-3, 3} and option D is {A, O}, each with two elements. Option A has no element at all, so it is the empty set, not a singleton.

questions.question: Which of the following is an infinite set?

options.c: {x : x is a state in Nigeria}
options.d: {x : x is a student registered at UNILAG in the 2025/26 session}

questions.explanation: The even integers ..., -4, -2, 0, 2, 4, ... go on without end, so they cannot be counted by any finite number. Option A may look long, but it stops at 1000, so it is a finite set with 1000 elements. The states of Nigeria in option C and the registered students in option D can also be counted, so those sets are finite too.

questions.question: Let A = {Lagos, Kano, Abuja} and B = {1, 2, 3}. Which statement about A and B is correct?

options.a: A and B are neither equal nor equivalent
options.b: A and B are equal sets
options.c: A and B are equivalent but not equal
options.d: A and B are equal but not equivalent

questions.explanation: Equivalent sets have the same number of elements, so their elements can be paired off one to one, and here n(A) = n(B) = 3. They are not equal, because equal sets must contain exactly the same elements and Lagos is not in B. Option B mixes up equal with equivalent, and option D is impossible because equal sets are always equivalent.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs of sets are equal?

options.b: {x : x is a letter of the word ABUJA} and {A, B, J, U}

questions.explanation: Repeated letters are listed only once and order does not matter, so the letters of ABUJA form exactly the set {A, B, J, U}. In option A the number 8 is in only one of the sets. In option C, {0} has one element while { } has none, and in option D the second set has just one element, the ordered pair (1, 2).

questions.question: Find n(A) if A = {x : x is an odd integer and 10 < x < 30}.
questions.explanation: The odd integers strictly between 10 and 30 are 11, 13, 15, ..., 29, which is (29 - 11)/2 + 1 = 10 numbers. Option C counts every integer from 11 to 29, odd and even alike. Options B and A come from off-by-one slips when counting the list.

questions.question: Let A = {1, 2, {3}}. Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.explanation: A has exactly three elements: 1, 2 and the set {3}. So {3} belongs to A, but the number 3 on its own does not, which rules out option A. Option B miscounts, since n(A) = 3, and option D is wrong because {1, 2} is a subset of A, not one of its elements.

questions.question: Which of the following is a subset of every set?
questions.explanation: The empty set has no element that could fail to belong to another set, so { } is a subset of every set. The universal set in option C contains the sets under discussion, so it is generally not a subset of a smaller set such as {1}. The sets {0} and {{ }} in options B and A each have one element, so they are subsets only of sets that contain that element.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the universal set U is correct?

options.a: A u U = A for every subset A of U
options.b: Every set under discussion is a subset of U
options.c: The complement of U is U itself
options.d: U is a subset of every set under discussion

questions.explanation: The universal set is the big set that contains all the sets in a given discussion, so each of them is a subset of U; for example, the integers can serve as U for the even and the odd integers. Option D describes the empty set, which is the set that is a subset of every set. Option A is wrong because A u U = U, and option C is wrong because U' = { }.

questions.question: When a set is written as A = {x : x is a vowel in the English alphabet}, the method used to describe it is the
questions.explanation: In the selector method the elements are not listed; they are described by a property that every member satisfies, such as 'x is a vowel'. The tabular method in option D would list the members as {a, e, i, o, u}. A Venn diagram (option B) is a picture of sets, and a Cartesian product (option C) is a set of ordered pairs, not a way of describing one set.

questions.question: Which of the following is a proper subset of A = {2, 4, 6, 8}?
questions.explanation: B is a proper subset of A when every element of B is in A and A has at least one element that is not in B, and {4, 8} meets both conditions. Option C is a subset of A but not a proper one, because it is equal to A. Options A and D are not subsets of A at all, since 5 and 10 are not in A.

questions.question: Let A = {N100, N200, N500, N1000} be a set of naira denominations. How many non-empty proper subsets does A have?
questions.explanation: A set with n = 4 elements has 2^4 = 16 subsets in all. Removing the empty set and A itself leaves 16 - 2 = 14 subsets that are both non-empty and proper. Option B counts every subset, and option C removes only one of the two sets that must be excluded.

questions.question: A bank in Lagos offers 5 optional add-on services: SMS alerts, a debit card, internet banking, a cheque book and USSD banking. A new customer may choose any combination of them, including none at all. How many different combinations are possible?
questions.explanation: Each possible choice is a subset of the set of 5 services, and the empty choice is allowed, so the number of combinations is the size of the power set, 2^5 = 32. Option D leaves out the choice of no service, which the question allows. Options C and A use 5^2 and 2 x 5 instead of 2^5.

questions.question: The power set of a set A has 128 elements. How many elements does A have?
questions.explanation: Since n(P(A)) = 2^n, we need 2^n = 128 = 2^7, so n = 7. Option B would give 2^6 = 64 subsets and option A would give 2^8 = 256, so neither fits. Option D simply halves 128 instead of solving 2^n = 128.

questions.question: How many elements does the power set of the empty set, P({ }), contain?
questions.explanation: The only subset of { } is { } itself, so P({ }) = {{ }}, a set with exactly one element, which agrees with 2^0 = 1. Option D confuses P({ }) with { }, which has no elements, and option C is the count for a set with one element, 2^1 = 2. The power set of every set, even the empty set, is defined, so option A is wrong.

questions.question: If A = {x, y}, which of the following is the power set P(A)?
questions.explanation: The power set lists every subset of A, including the empty set { } and A itself, and there must be 2^2 = 4 of them: { }, {x}, {y} and {x, y}. Option D leaves out the empty set, and option C leaves out A itself as well. Option A has four items, but x and y are elements of A, not subsets, so they must appear as {x} and {y}.

questions.question: If n(A) = 2 and n(B) = 3, how many subsets does the Cartesian product A x B have?
questions.explanation: First, n(A x B) = n(A) x n(B) = 2 x 3 = 6 ordered pairs, and a set with 6 elements has 2^6 = 64 subsets. Option A uses 2^(2 + 3) = 32, adding the sizes of A and B instead of multiplying them. Option B squares 6 instead of raising 2 to the power 6.

questions.question: A set A has 2 more elements than a set B, and the power set of A has 48 more elements than the power set of B. Find n(B).
questions.explanation: If n(B) = m, then n(P(A)) - n(P(B)) = 2^(m + 2) - 2^m = 4(2^m) - 2^m = 3(2^m). Setting 3(2^m) = 48 gives 2^m = 16, so m = 4; check: 2^6 - 2^4 = 64 - 16 = 48. Option C is n(A), not n(B), and option D is the number of subsets of B rather than its number of elements.

questions.question: Let A = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10} and B = {4, 8, 12, 16}. Find the symmetric difference A Delta B = (A - B) u (B - A).
questions.explanation: A - B = {2, 6, 10} and B - A = {12, 16}, so A Delta B = {2, 6, 10, 12, 16}, the elements that lie in exactly one of the two sets. Option A is A n B, the elements the sets share. Option D is only A - B, and option C is the whole union A u B.

questions.question: For two sets A and B, n(A) = 40, n(B) = 30 and n(A n B) = 12. Find n(A Delta B), where A Delta B = (A - B) u (B - A) is the symmetric difference.
questions.explanation: A Delta B holds the elements in A or B but not in both, so n(A Delta B) = n(A - B) + n(B - A) = (40 - 12) + (30 - 12) = 28 + 18 = 46. Option D is n(A u B) = 58, which still includes the 12 common elements. Option B is only n(A - B), and option A adds n(A) and n(B) with no adjustment at all.

questions.question: If U = {1, 2, 3, ..., 12} and A = {x : x is a multiple of 3}, where A is a subset of U, find A'.
questions.explanation: A = {3, 6, 9, 12}, and A' = U - A contains every element of U that is not in A, namely {1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 11}. Option A is A itself, not its complement. Option C leaves out 11, and option B includes 0, which is not in U.

questions.question: In a survey of UNILAG students, L is the set of students who own a laptop and P is the set of students who own a smartphone. The set L - P is the set of students who

options.a: own both a laptop and a smartphone
options.b: own a laptop or a smartphone
options.c: own a laptop but not a smartphone
options.d: own a smartphone but not a laptop

questions.explanation: L - P contains the members of L that are not in P, which is the same set as L n P'. Option D describes P - L, the difference taken the other way round. Options A and B describe L n P and L u P.

questions.question: In a survey of traders at Onitsha Main Market, A is the set of traders who accept bank transfers and B is the set who accept POS payments. Which set describes the traders who accept neither bank transfers nor POS payments?
questions.explanation: Accepting neither means being outside A and also outside B, which is A' n B'; by De Morgan's law this is the same as (A u B)'. Option C, A' u B', equals (A n B)', so it also includes traders who accept just one of the two methods. Option A describes traders who accept exactly one method, and option D those who accept both.

questions.question: For any two sets A and B in a universal set U, the difference A - B is equal to
questions.explanation: A - B consists of the elements that are in A and not in B, that is, in A and in B', which is A n B'. Option B describes B - A instead. Option C is much larger, since it includes everything outside B, even elements outside A, and option D includes everything that is not in both sets.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT equal to the symmetric difference A Delta B of two sets A and B?
questions.explanation: A - B and B - A never share an element, so (A - B) n (B - A) is always the empty set and is not the symmetric difference in general. Options C and B are two standard ways of writing A Delta B, the elements that are in exactly one of the sets. Option D is also equal to it, because A Delta B = B Delta A.

questions.question: Two sets A and B are said to be disjoint if

options.a: A is a subset of B

questions.explanation: Disjoint sets have no element in common, so their intersection is empty: A n B = { }, as with {a, b} and {p, q}. Option B would force both sets to be empty. Option D describes equivalent finite sets, and option A describes a subset, where every element of A is shared with B.

questions.question: Let A = {1, 2, 3, ..., 10}, B = {2, 4, 6, 8} and C = {3, 6, 9}. Find A - (B u C).
questions.explanation: B u C = {2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9}, and removing these elements from A leaves {1, 5, 7, 10}; this also equals (A - B) n (A - C). Option C is (A - B) u (A - C), which uses a union where an intersection is needed. Option A removes only the elements of B, and option B is B n C.

questions.question: The identity A u (B n C) = (A u B) n (A u C) is known as the
questions.explanation: Union is being distributed over intersection, much as multiplication distributes over addition in a(b + c) = ab + ac, so this is the distributive law. De Morgan's laws (option C) involve complements, such as (A u B)' = A' n B'. The commutative law (option D) only swaps order, A u B = B u A, and the associative law (option B) regroups, A u (B u C) = (A u B) u C.

questions.question: Which of the following illustrates the commutative law of sets?

options.b: A n (B n C) = (A n B) n C
options.c: A n (B u C) = (A n B) u (A n C)
options.d: A n B = B n A

questions.explanation: The commutative law says the order of the two sets does not matter, so A n B = B n A, and likewise A u B = B u A. Option B is the associative law, which regroups three sets. Option C is the distributive law, and option A is one of De Morgan's laws.

questions.question: By De Morgan's law, the complement of the union of two sets, (A u B)', is equal to
questions.explanation: An element lies outside A u B exactly when it lies outside A and also outside B, so (A u B)' = A' n B'. Option D is the other De Morgan law, which gives (A n B)', not (A u B)'. Option A takes the complement of A only, and option B has no complement at all.

questions.question: In a universal set U, n(U) = 150, n(A) = 70, n(B) = 50 and n(A u B) = 85. Find n(A' u B').
questions.explanation: By De Morgan's law A' u B' = (A n B)', so first find n(A n B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A u B) = 70 + 50 - 85 = 35. Then n(A' u B') = n(U) - n(A n B) = 150 - 35 = 115. Option D is n(A' n B') = 150 - 85, which uses the wrong De Morgan law, and option A adds n(A') + n(B') = 80 + 100 without removing their overlap.

questions.question: Which of the following set identities is NOT true for all sets A, B and C?

options.c: A u B = B u A
options.d: A n (B u C) = (A n B) u (A n C)

questions.explanation: Set difference is not commutative: with A = {1, 3, 5} and B = {4, 5, 6}, A - B = {1, 3} but B - A = {4, 6}. Option D is the distributive law, option B is De Morgan's law and option C is the commutative law for union, and each of these holds for every choice of sets.

questions.question: Let A = {1, 2, 3, 4}, B = {3, 4, 5} and C = {4, 5, 6}. Find A n (B u C), which by the distributive law equals (A n B) u (A n C).
questions.explanation: B u C = {3, 4, 5, 6}, and the elements of A that lie in this set are 3 and 4, so A n (B u C) = {3, 4}. As a check, (A n B) u (A n C) = {3, 4} u {4} = {3, 4}. Option B is A n B n C, and option A is B u C before intersecting with A.

questions.question: If A = {1, 2, 3}, B = {p, q} and C = {q, r}, how many ordered pairs are in A x (B u C)?
questions.explanation: B u C = {p, q, r} has 3 elements, so n(A x (B u C)) = 3 x 3 = 9; this matches n((A x B) u (A x C)) = 6 + 6 - 3. Option A uses n(B) + n(C) = 4 without removing the shared element q. Option B counts A x (B n C), where B n C = {q}.

questions.question: Each of the 60 traders in one section of Balogun Market sells shoes, bags or both. If 38 sell shoes and 31 sell bags, how many sell both?
questions.explanation: Since every trader sells at least one item, n(S u B) = 60, so n(S n B) = n(S) + n(B) - n(S u B) = 38 + 31 - 60 = 9. Option C simply adds 38 and 31, which counts the 9 traders twice. Options D and B are 60 - 38 and 60 - 31, the numbers who sell only bags and only shoes.

questions.question: In a survey of 250 UNILAG students, 140 use MTN lines, 120 use Airtel lines and 45 use both. How many of the students use MTN only?
questions.explanation: Students who use MTN only are in the MTN set but not in the Airtel set, so the number is 140 - 45 = 95. Option C is the total number of MTN users, which still includes the 45 who also use Airtel. Option A is the number who use Airtel only, 120 - 45, and option D is the number who use at least one network, 140 + 120 - 45.

questions.question: A supermarket in Ikeja recorded 300 customers in one day: 180 bought rice, 150 bought beans and 60 bought neither. How many customers bought exactly one of the two items?
questions.explanation: At least one item was bought by 300 - 60 = 240 customers, so the number who bought both is 180 + 150 - 240 = 90. Exactly one item means rice only plus beans only: (180 - 90) + (150 - 90) = 90 + 60 = 150. Option B is everyone who bought at least one item, which still includes the 90 who bought both, and option D is 300 - 90, which wrongly includes the 60 who bought neither.

questions.question: In a survey of small business owners in Ibadan, 72% use Opay, 48% use Palmpay and 30% use both apps. What percentage of the owners use neither app?
questions.explanation: The share using at least one app is 72% + 48% - 30% = 90%, so 100% - 90% = 10% use neither. Option C is the 90% who use at least one app. Option D subtracts only the one-app users (42% + 18%) from 100%, so it wrongly keeps the 30% who use both, and option A is the share who use Opay only.

questions.question: Each of the 85 staff of a Victoria Island firm uses at least one of the ride-hailing apps Uber and Bolt. If 50 use Uber and 20 use both apps, how many staff use Bolt?
questions.explanation: With n(Uber u Bolt) = n(Uber) + n(Bolt) - n(both), we get 85 = 50 + n(Bolt) - 20, so n(Bolt) = 55. Option B is 85 - 50 = 35, the number who use Bolt only, which leaves out the 20 who use both apps. Option D subtracts the 20 instead of adding them back.

questions.question: A survey of 200 shoppers at a Lagos mall reports that 150 bought noodles and 120 bought pasta. For these figures to be consistent with a total of 200 shoppers, at least how many shoppers must have bought both products?
questions.explanation: Since n(N u P) cannot exceed the 200 shoppers, n(N n P) = n(N) + n(P) - n(N u P) must be at least 150 + 120 - 200 = 70. Any smaller overlap would make n(N u P) larger than 200, so options D and B are impossible. Option C, 120, is the largest possible overlap, not the smallest.

questions.question: In a survey of 1,000 voters in Abeokuta, it was reported that 400 read The Punch, 350 read Vanguard, 120 read both papers and 380 read neither. Are these figures consistent?

options.a: No; they account for 1,130 voters, not 1,000
options.b: Yes; they account for exactly 1,000 voters
options.c: No; they account for 1,010 voters, not 1,000
options.d: Yes; because 120 is less than both 400 and 350

questions.explanation: The number reading at least one paper is 400 + 350 - 120 = 630, and adding the 380 who read neither gives 630 + 380 = 1,010. This is more than the 1,000 voters surveyed, so the figures are inconsistent. Option A reaches 1,130 by forgetting to subtract the 120 who read both, and option D checks only one condition, which is not enough.

questions.question: In a survey of Lagos commuters, 60% use BRT buses and 45% use danfo buses, and every commuter surveyed uses at least one of the two. What percentage use BRT buses only?
questions.explanation: Since everyone uses at least one, n(B n D) = 60% + 45% - 100% = 5%, so BRT only = 60% - 5% = 55%; equivalently, everyone who does not use danfo must use BRT only, 100% - 45% = 55%. Option D is the 5% who use both, and option A is the total share of BRT users, which still includes that 5%. Option B is the share who use danfo only, 45% - 5%.

questions.question: In the formula n(A u B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A n B), the term n(A n B) is subtracted because

options.a: elements in both A and B are counted twice in n(A) + n(B)
options.b: elements outside A and B must be removed from the total
options.c: A and B are always disjoint sets
options.d: elements in A but not in B are counted twice in n(A) + n(B)

questions.explanation: An element that belongs to both sets is counted once in n(A) and again in n(B), so subtracting n(A n B) once leaves every element counted exactly once. Option C is wrong, because for disjoint sets n(A n B) = 0 and the formula reduces to n(A u B) = n(A) + n(B). Option D is wrong since elements of A only appear in n(A) alone, and option B describes finding 'neither', which uses n(U) - n(A u B).

questions.question: For two sets A and B, n(A u B) = 60, n(A - B) = 22 and n(B - A) = 18. Find n(A n B).
questions.explanation: A u B splits into three non-overlapping parts: A only, B only and both, so n(A n B) = 60 - 22 - 18 = 20, giving n(A) = 42 and n(B) = 38. Option A is n(A Delta B) = 22 + 18, the elements in exactly one set. Option C is n(B) = 60 - 22, which still includes the part of B shared with A.

questions.question: A company in Ilorin has 120 employees. 70 speak Yoruba, 55 speak Hausa and 20 speak neither language. How many employees speak both Yoruba and Hausa?
questions.explanation: The employees who speak at least one of the languages number 120 - 20 = 100, so the number who speak both is 70 + 55 - 100 = 25. Option D uses 120 in place of n(Y u H), forgetting the 20 who speak neither. Option B is the number who speak Yoruba only, 70 - 25, and option C is the number who speak at least one language.

questions.question: In a survey of 500 UNILAG students on how they follow the news, 230 use television (T), 180 use radio (R) and 290 use the internet (I). 70 use T and R, 110 use T and I, 90 use R and I, and 40 use all three. How many students use exactly two of the three?
questions.explanation: Each pairwise figure includes the 40 who use all three, so the exactly-two regions are 70 - 40 = 30, 110 - 40 = 70 and 90 - 40 = 50, giving 30 + 70 + 50 = 150. Option B adds 70 + 110 + 90 without removing the triple overlap, and option A subtracts the 40 only once. Option D is the number who use at least two, 150 + 40.

questions.question: A bank branch in Surulere has 400 customers, each holding at least one of a savings (S), current (C) or fixed-deposit (F) account. 250 hold S, 170 hold C and 125 hold F; 70 hold S and C, 55 hold S and F, and 45 hold C and F. How many customers hold all three types of account?
questions.explanation: Using n(S u C u F) = n(S) + n(C) + n(F) - n(S n C) - n(S n F) - n(C n F) + n(S n C n F), we get 400 = 250 + 170 + 125 - 70 - 55 - 45 + x = 375 + x, so x = 25. Option B is 375, the value of the formula before the triple term is added. Option C is 545 - 400, which ignores the pairwise overlaps completely.

questions.question: A survey of 200 small businesses in Aba found that 77 advertise on Facebook (F), 70 on Instagram (I) and 110 on WhatsApp (W). 27 use F and I, 32 use F and W, 30 use I and W, and 12 use all three. How many businesses advertise on WhatsApp only?
questions.explanation: WhatsApp only = n(W) - n(F n W) - n(I n W) + n(F n I n W) = 110 - 32 - 30 + 12 = 60. The 12 businesses on all three platforms are removed twice when both pairwise figures are subtracted, so they must be added back once. Option D forgets to add them back, and option B subtracts them a third time.

questions.question: A survey of 200 small businesses in Aba found that 77 advertise on Facebook (F), 70 on Instagram (I) and 110 on WhatsApp (W). 27 use F and I, 32 use F and W, 30 use I and W, and 12 use all three. How many businesses advertise on at least two of the three platforms?
questions.explanation: At least two means exactly two or all three. The exactly-two regions are 27 - 12 = 15, 32 - 12 = 20 and 30 - 12 = 18, so the total is 15 + 20 + 18 + 12 = 65. Option D adds 27 + 32 + 30 = 89, which counts the 12 three times, and option C is 53, the number on exactly two platforms only.

questions.question: A report on 100 customers of a Kaduna supermarket states that 50 bought bread (B), 45 bought milk (M) and 40 bought sugar (S); 30 bought B and M, 28 bought B and S, 20 bought M and S, and 5 bought all three. Find the number who bought bread only, and decide whether the report is consistent.

options.a: -3, but the report is consistent because n(B u M u S) = 62 does not exceed 100

questions.explanation: Bread only = n(B) - n(B n M) - n(B n S) + n(B n M n S) = 50 - 30 - 28 + 5 = -3. No region of a Venn diagram can hold a negative number of customers, so the report is inconsistent. Option A is a trap: the total n(B u M u S) = 62 does fit within 100, but every region must also be non-negative, and option C subtracts the 5 instead of adding it back.

questions.question: For any three finite sets A, B and C, n(A u B u C) is equal to

options.a: n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A n B) - n(A n C) - n(B n C) + n(A n B n C)
options.b: n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A n B) - n(A n C) - n(B n C)
options.c: n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A n B) - n(A n C) - n(B n C) - n(A n B n C)
options.d: n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A n B n C)

questions.explanation: Adding n(A), n(B) and n(C) counts the triple overlap three times, and subtracting the three pairwise intersections removes it three times, so n(A n B n C) must be added back once. Option B stops before this step and leaves the triple overlap uncounted, while option C removes it once more. Option D ignores the elements shared by exactly two sets, which would then be counted twice.

questions.question: A logistics firm delivers from the cities A = {Lagos, Ibadan, Abeokuta, Ilorin} using the modes B = {van, train, motorbike}. How many (city, mode) ordered pairs are in A x B?
questions.explanation: Each of the 4 cities can be paired with each of the 3 modes, so n(A x B) = n(A) x n(B) = 4 x 3 = 12. Option A adds the sizes instead of multiplying them. Option D counts the pairs of A x B and B x A together, but only pairs with the city first belong to A x B.

questions.question: If n(A x B) = 35 and n(A) = 7, find n(B).
questions.explanation: Since n(A x B) = n(A) x n(B), we have 7 x n(B) = 35, so n(B) = 35/7 = 5. Option C subtracts 7 from 35, treating the size of the product as if it were a sum. Option A multiplies 35 by 7 instead of dividing.

questions.question: Let A = {1, 2} and B = {a, b}. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.a: (1, a) is in A x B but not in B x A
options.b: A x B = B x A

questions.explanation: In A x B the first entry comes from A and the second from B, so (1, a) is in A x B, while every pair in B x A starts with a or b. Ordered pairs are equal only when their first entries match and their second entries match, so (1, a) is not equal to (a, 1), which rules out option C. For the same reason A x B is not equal to B x A (option B), and (a, 1) belongs to B x A, not A x B (option D).

questions.question: If (3x + 2, 14) = (11, 2y - 4), find the values of x and y.
questions.explanation: Two ordered pairs are equal only when their first entries are equal and their second entries are equal. So 3x + 2 = 11 gives x = 3, and 14 = 2y - 4 gives 2y = 18 and y = 9. Option A comes from a sign slip, solving 2y = 14 - 4, and option B swaps the values of x and y.

questions.question: If A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {2, 3, 4}, how many ordered pairs are in (A x B) n (B x A)?
questions.explanation: A pair (x, y) lies in both products only if x and y each lie in A n B = {2, 3}, so (A x B) n (B x A) = {(2, 2), (2, 3), (3, 2), (3, 3)}, which has 4 elements. Option D is the size of A x B on its own, and option A is n(A n B). Option B assumes A x B and B x A can share no pairs, which is true only when A and B have no common element.

questions.question: If A = {1, 2, 3} and B = { }, the empty set, how many elements does A x B have?
questions.explanation: Every ordered pair in A x B needs a second entry taken from B, and B has no elements, so no pair can be formed and A x B = { }. This agrees with n(A x B) = n(A) x n(B) = 3 x 0 = 0. Option D adds instead of multiplying (3 + 0 = 3), and option A treats the empty set as if it had one element.

questions.question: A firm's possible unit costs are A = {N200, N300, N500} and its possible unit selling prices are B = {N250, N300, N600}. How many pairs (cost, selling price) in A x B give the firm a profit?
questions.explanation: A pair gives a profit only when the selling price is greater than the cost: (N200, N250), (N200, N300), (N200, N600), (N300, N600) and (N500, N600), so there are 5. Option B also counts (N300, N300), but selling at cost gives zero profit, not a profit. Option A counts all 3 x 3 = 9 pairs of A x B.

questions.question: For a product, demand is D = 20 - 2p and supply is S = 3p - 5, where p is the price in naira and p = 1, 2, ..., 8. Using set theory, the equilibrium is the ordered pair common to the sets {(p, D)} and {(p, S)}. Which pair is it?
questions.explanation: Listing the pairs gives {(p, D)} = {(1, 18), (2, 16), ..., (5, 10), ...} and {(p, S)} = {(1, -2), (2, 1), ..., (5, 10), ...}, and the only pair in both sets is (5, 10). So the equilibrium price is N5 and the quantity is 10 units, since 20 - 2(5) = 3(5) - 5 = 10. Option D is on the demand list only and option C is on the supply list only, while option A reverses the order of price and quantity.

questions.question: If consumption is N6 billion when disposable income is 0, and if the marginal propensity to consume is dC/dy = 0.3 + 0.4/sqrt(y) (in billions of naira), find the national consumption function, if C = 6 and y = 0.
questions.explanation: Consumption is the integral of the MPC: C = integral of (0.3 + 0.4y^(-1/2)) dy = 0.3y + 0.4 x 2y^(1/2) + K = 0.3y + 0.8sqrt(y) + K, and C = 6 when y = 0 gives K = 6. Options B and D forget that the constant 0.3 integrates to 0.3y, and option C has the wrong coefficient (0.6) and leaves K undetermined.

questions.question: If consumption is N9 billion when disposable income is 0, and if the marginal propensity to save is 0.25, find the consumption function, if C = 9 and y = 0.
questions.explanation: Since MPC + MPS = 1, the MPC is 1 - 0.25 = 0.75, so C = integral of 0.75 dy = 0.75y + K, and C = 9 when y = 0 gives K = 9: C = 0.75y + 9. Option D has the right slope but leaves the constant unevaluated, and option B uses 0.5 instead of 0.75.

questions.question: With C = f(Y), the marginal propensity to consume is given by MPC = dC/dY = f'(Y). If the MPC = 0.8, consumption = 40 when income is zero, find the consumption function.
questions.explanation: Integrating the MPC gives C = integral of 0.8 dY = 0.8Y + K, and consumption of 40 at zero income (autonomous consumption) means K = 40, so C = 0.8Y + 40. Option A leaves the constant unevaluated, and options C and D change the MPC from 0.8 to 0.6 or 8.

questions.question: Given dC/dY = 0.6 + 0.1/(Y^(1/3)) = MPC and C = 45 when Y = 0. Find the consumption function.
questions.explanation: Integrate term by term: the integral of 0.6 is 0.6Y and the integral of 0.1Y^(-1/3) is 0.1 x Y^(2/3)/(2/3) = 0.15Y^(2/3), so C = 0.6Y + 0.15Y^(2/3) + K. Since C = 45 when Y = 0, K = 45. Option D uses the wrong constant (35), option B leaves the constant unevaluated, and option A forgets that 0.6 integrates to 0.6Y.

questions.question: The marginal propensity to save is given by dS/dY = 0.5 - 0.2Y^(-1/2). There is dissaving of 3.5 when income is 25, that is, S = -3.5 when Y = 25. Find the savings function.
questions.explanation: Integrating, S = 0.5Y - 0.2 x Y^(1/2)/(1/2) + K = 0.5Y - 0.4Y^(1/2) + K. Using S = -3.5 at Y = 25: 0.5(25) - 0.4(5) + K = -3.5, so 10.5 + K = -3.5 and K = -14. Option B has the sign of the constant wrong (+14), while options A and D leave it unevaluated or out.

questions.question: If the marginal propensity to save is dS/dy = 0.7 - 0.4/sqrt(y), find the marginal propensity to consume.
questions.explanation: Every extra naira of income is either consumed or saved, so MPC + MPS = 1 and MPC = 1 - (0.7 - 0.4/sqrt(y)) = 0.3 + 0.4/sqrt(y). Subtracting from 1 only turns 0.7 into 0.3 and flips the sign of the 0.4/sqrt(y) term; Option C wrongly changes the 0.4 to 0.3, and Options B and D wrongly put 2y under the square root.

questions.question: Find an expression for the savings function if the marginal propensity to save is given by MPS = 0.4 - 0.1Y^(-1/2) and savings are zero when income is 100.
questions.explanation: Integrate the MPS: S = 0.4Y - 0.1Y^(1/2)/(1/2) + c = 0.4Y - 0.2Y^(1/2) + c. Since S = 0 when Y = 100, 0 = 40 - 0.2(10) + c, so c = -38 and S = 0.4Y - 0.2Y^(1/2) - 38. Option A has the wrong sign on the constant, Option B changes the sign of the square-root term, and Option C multiplies by 1/2 instead of dividing by it when integrating Y^(-1/2).

questions.question: If C = f(Y) is a consumption function, where C is consumption and Y is income, the marginal propensity to consume (MPC) is defined as
questions.explanation: The MPC measures how much consumption changes when income changes by a small amount, so it is the derivative dC/dY = f'(Y). Option C, C/Y, is the average propensity to consume, not the marginal one. Option D, dS/dY, is the marginal propensity to save, and option B is just the APC turned upside down.

questions.question: Income is either consumed or saved, so Y = C + S. Differentiating both sides with respect to Y gives which relationship?
questions.explanation: Differentiating Y = C + S with respect to Y gives 1 = dC/dY + dS/dY, that is MPC + MPS = 1, so each extra naira of income is split between extra consumption and extra saving. Option B has a sign error, and option A multiplies the two propensities when they should be added. Option D confuses the derivative of Y, which is 1, with Y itself.

questions.question: Which pair correctly defines the average propensity to consume (APC) and the average propensity to save (APS) at income level Y?
questions.explanation: Average propensities are simple ratios to income: APC = C/Y is the fraction of income consumed and APS = S/Y is the fraction saved, so APC + APS = 1. Option B gives the marginal propensities, which are derivatives rather than ratios. Options C and D turn the ratios upside down or divide by the wrong quantity.

questions.question: In the linear consumption function C = a + bY, where 0 < b < 1, the constant a represents

options.a: The break-even income at which consumption equals Y
options.b: The marginal propensity to consume out of income
options.c: The average propensity to consume at every income
options.d: Autonomous consumption, i.e. consumption when Y = 0

questions.explanation: Setting Y = 0 in C = a + bY gives C = a, so a is autonomous consumption, the amount consumed even when income is zero. Option B is wrong because the MPC is the slope b, not the intercept. Option C is wrong because APC = C/Y = a/Y + b changes with income, and option A describes the income a/(1 - b) at which C = Y.

questions.question: For the consumption function C = 60 + 0.7Y, where C and Y are in N billion and MPC = dC/dY, which of the following statements is NOT true?
questions.explanation: The statement that APC = 0.7 at every income level is the false one: APC = C/Y = 60/Y + 0.7, which is always above 0.7 and falls as income rises. The other three are true: MPC = dC/dY = 0.7 (option C), MPS = 1 - 0.7 = 0.3 (option A), and S = Y - C = 0.3Y - 60 (option B).

questions.question: For a linear consumption function C = a + bY with a > 0 and 0 < b < 1, what happens to the average propensity to consume (APC) as income Y increases?

options.a: It stays constant and equal to b
options.b: It rises and gets closer to 1
options.c: It falls and gets closer to b
options.d: It rises and gets closer to b

questions.explanation: APC = (a + bY)/Y = a/Y + b, and as Y grows the term a/Y shrinks towards zero, so the APC falls and gets closer to the MPC b while staying above it. Option B wrongly assumes a larger fraction of income is spent as income grows, and option A confuses the APC with the MPC, which is the constant b. Option D gets the limit right but the direction wrong.

questions.question: Given the consumption function C = 120 + 0.65Y, where C and Y are in N billion, which of the following is the corresponding saving function?
questions.explanation: Saving is income not consumed: S = Y - C = Y - (120 + 0.65Y) = 0.35Y - 120, so there is dissaving of N120 billion when income is zero. Option C gets the sign of the intercept wrong, and option D uses the MPC of 0.65 as the slope of saving instead of the MPS of 1 - 0.65 = 0.35. Option B reverses every sign, which would make saving fall as income rises.

questions.question: A household in Ibadan has the monthly consumption function C = 180 + 0.6Y, where C and Y are in thousands of naira. At what monthly income does the household consume exactly all of its income (C = Y)?
questions.explanation: Break-even income is where C = Y: Y = 180 + 0.6Y gives 0.4Y = 180, so Y = 450 thousand naira, i.e. N450,000. Option C divides 180 by the MPC (0.6) instead of the MPS (1 - 0.6 = 0.4), and option A divides by 1 + 0.6 after a sign slip. Option B multiplies 180 by 1.6 instead of dividing.

questions.question: The aggregate consumption function of a state economy is C = 240 + 0.7Y, where C and Y are in N billion. Find the average propensity to consume when income is N1,200 billion. (Correct to 2 decimal places.)
questions.explanation: At Y = 1,200, C = 240 + 0.7(1,200) = 1,080, so APC = C/Y = 1,080/1,200 = 0.90. Option B is the MPC, the slope of the function, which differs from the average ratio when there is autonomous consumption. Option A is the APS (1 - 0.90), and option D is Y/C, the ratio turned upside down.

questions.question: An economy has the consumption function C = 50 + 0.75Y, where C and Y are in N billion. Find the average propensity to save (APS) when income is N400 billion.
questions.explanation: At Y = 400, C = 50 + 0.75(400) = 350, so S = Y - C = 400 - 350 = 50 and APS = S/Y = 50/400 = 0.125. Option C comes from computing saving as C - Y, a sign slip. Option A is the MPS (1 - 0.75), and option D is the APC, 350/400.

questions.question: An economy has the consumption function C = 100 + 0.8Y, where C and Y are in N billion. What is the level of saving when income is N300 billion?
questions.explanation: S = Y - C = 300 - (100 + 0.8 x 300) = 300 - 340 = -40, so the economy dissaves N40 billion because income is below the break-even level of 100/0.2 = 500. Option B drops the minus sign, option D uses only 0.2Y and forgets the autonomous consumption, and option C is the saving at zero income rather than at Y = 300.

questions.question: An economy has the consumption function C = 120 + 0.7Y, where C and Y are in N billion. At what level of income is the average propensity to consume equal to 0.85? (Correct to 2 decimal places where necessary.)
questions.explanation: APC = C/Y = 120/Y + 0.7, so setting 120/Y + 0.7 = 0.85 gives 120/Y = 0.15 and Y = N800 billion. Option B is the break-even income 120/0.3, where the APC equals 1, not 0.85. Options A and D divide 120 by 0.85 or by 0.7 instead of by 0.85 - 0.7 = 0.15.

questions.question: In an economy, consumption is N190 billion when income is N200 billion, and N265 billion when income is N300 billion. Assuming a linear consumption function C = a + bY, which is the consumption function?
questions.explanation: The slope is MPC = (265 - 190)/(300 - 200) = 75/100 = 0.75, and then a = 190 - 0.75(200) = 40, so C = 40 + 0.75Y (check: 40 + 0.75 x 300 = 265). Option D uses the first consumption figure as the intercept, and option B uses the MPS 0.25 as the slope. Option A has a sign slip in the intercept: 190 - 150 is +40, not -40.

questions.question: A household's marginal propensity to save is constant at 0.2. It saves N30,000 a month when its monthly income is N400,000. Find its autonomous consumption (its consumption when income is zero).
questions.explanation: With MPS constant, S = 0.2Y + k, and S = 30,000 at Y = 400,000 gives 30,000 = 80,000 + k, so k = -50,000. Then C = Y - S = 0.8Y + 50,000, so autonomous consumption is N50,000. Option B takes the saving figure itself as the answer, option D is just 0.2 x 400,000, and option A adds 80,000 and 30,000 instead of subtracting.

questions.question: The consumption function of an economy is C = 30 + 0.7Y + 0.6sqrt(Y), where C and Y are in N billion. Find the marginal propensity to consume, MPC = dC/dY, when income is N100 billion.
questions.explanation: Differentiate term by term: d/dY(0.6Y^(1/2)) = 0.3Y^(-1/2), so MPC = 0.7 + 0.3/sqrt(Y), and at Y = 100 it is 0.7 + 0.3/10 = 0.73. Option B forgets to multiply by the power 1/2 and gets 0.7 + 0.6/10 = 0.76. Option A ignores the square-root term, and option C is the MPS, 1 - 0.73.

questions.question: The marginal propensity to consume of an economy is MPC = 0.6 + 0.2/sqrt(Y), where income Y is in N billion. Find the marginal propensity to save when income is N16 billion.
questions.explanation: At Y = 16, MPC = 0.6 + 0.2/sqrt(16) = 0.6 + 0.05 = 0.65, and since MPC + MPS = 1, MPS = 1 - 0.65 = 0.35. Option C stops at the MPC, option D subtracts only the constant 0.6 and forgets the 0.05, and option B adds the 0.05 instead of subtracting it.

questions.question: The marginal propensity to consume of an economy is MPC = dC/dY = 0.7 + 0.2Y^(-1/2), where C and Y are in N billion, and consumption is N80 billion when income is zero. Find consumption when income is N100 billion.
questions.explanation: Integrating gives C = 0.7Y + 0.2Y^(1/2)/(1/2) + k = 0.7Y + 0.4Y^(1/2) + k, and C = 80 at Y = 0 gives k = 80. So C(100) = 70 + 0.4(10) + 80 = N154 billion. Option D forgets to divide by the new power 1/2 (keeping 0.2Y^(1/2)), option B drops the square-root term, and option C leaves out the constant k = 80.

questions.question: The marginal propensity to consume of an economy is MPC = dC/dY = 0.6 + 0.3/sqrt(Y), where C and Y are in N billion. If income rises from N100 billion to N400 billion, by how much does consumption rise?
questions.explanation: The change in consumption is the integral of the MPC between the two incomes: [0.6Y + 0.6Y^(1/2)] from 100 to 400 = (240 + 12) - (60 + 6) = N186 billion. Option A forgets that integrating Y^(-1/2) gives 2Y^(1/2), option B ignores the square-root term, and option C is the rise in saving, 300 - 186 = 114.

questions.question: The consumption function of an economy is C = 10 + 0.75Y + 1.5sqrt(Y), where C and Y are in N billion. At what level of income is total saving, S = Y - C, smallest?
questions.explanation: Saving is S = 0.25Y - 1.5Y^(1/2) - 10, so dS/dY = 0.25 - 0.75Y^(-1/2), and setting this to zero gives sqrt(Y) = 3, so Y = N9 billion; d^2S/dY^2 = 0.375Y^(-3/2) > 0 confirms a minimum. Option A comes from differentiating 1.5Y^(1/2) as 1.5Y^(-1/2) (forgetting the 1/2), which gives sqrt(Y) = 6. Option D stops at sqrt(Y) = 3 without squaring, and option B stops at sqrt(Y) = 6 in the same faulty working as option A.

questions.question: A student is given MPC = dC/dY = 0.65 + 0.12Y^(-1/2), with C = 30 when Y = 0, and works as follows. Step 1: C = integral of (0.65 + 0.12Y^(-1/2)) dY. Step 2: C = 0.65Y + 0.06Y^(1/2) + k. Step 3: At Y = 0, C = 30, so k = 30. Step 4: C = 0.65Y + 0.06Y^(1/2) + 30. Which is the first incorrect step?
questions.explanation: Integrating 0.12Y^(-1/2) gives 0.12Y^(1/2)/(1/2) = 0.24Y^(1/2), not 0.06Y^(1/2), so Step 2 is the first error: the student multiplied by 1/2 instead of dividing. Step 1 (option A) correctly sets up C as the integral of the MPC, and Step 3 (option C) correctly uses C = 30 at Y = 0 to get k = 30. Step 4 (option D) is also wrong, but only because it carries forward the mistake from Step 2; the correct function is C = 0.65Y + 0.24Y^(1/2) + 30.

questions.question: In a simple economy where national income is Y = C + I, the consumption function is C = 400 + 0.8Y (N billion). What is the value of the investment multiplier?
questions.explanation: The investment multiplier is k = 1/(1 - MPC) = 1/(1 - 0.8) = 1/0.2 = 5, so each extra N1 of investment raises equilibrium income by N5. Option B uses 1/MPC, option C uses MPC/MPS = 0.8/0.2, and option A is the MPS itself.

questions.question: In a simple economy where Y = C + I, the marginal propensity to save is 0.25. If private investment rises by N15 billion, by how much does equilibrium national income rise?
questions.explanation: The multiplier is 1/(1 - MPC) = 1/MPS = 1/0.25 = 4, so equilibrium income rises by 4 x 15 = N60 billion. Option B divides by the MPC (0.75) instead of the MPS, option C uses MPC/MPS = 3 as the multiplier, and option A is just 0.75 x 15, the first-round rise in consumption.

questions.question: In a simple economy, national income is Y = C + I, with consumption C = 200 + 0.75Y and investment I = 300, all in N billion. Find the equilibrium level of national income. (Correct to 2 decimal places where necessary.)
questions.explanation: At equilibrium Y = 200 + 0.75Y + 300, so 0.25Y = 500 and Y = N2,000 billion. Option B divides 500 by the MPC (0.75) instead of the MPS (0.25). Options D and A each leave out one of the two autonomous amounts, using only 200 or only 300 over 0.25.

questions.question: In a simple economy, Y = C + I, with consumption C = 150 + 0.6Y and investment I = 90, all in N billion. Find the level of consumption at equilibrium.
questions.explanation: First find equilibrium income: Y = 150 + 0.6Y + 90 gives 0.4Y = 240, so Y = 600; then C = 150 + 0.6(600) = N510 billion (check: 510 + 90 = 600). Option B is equilibrium income, not consumption, and option A is only the induced part 0.6Y without the autonomous 150. Option C is 150 + 90, the total autonomous spending.

questions.question: The marginal propensity to consume of an economy is MPC = dC/dY = 0.25 + 1/sqrt(Y + 9), where C and Y are in N billion, and consumption is N10 billion when income is zero. Find the consumption function.
questions.explanation: The integral of (Y + 9)^(-1/2) is (Y + 9)^(1/2)/(1/2) = 2sqrt(Y + 9), so C = 0.25Y + 2sqrt(Y + 9) + k. At Y = 0, 10 = 2sqrt(9) + k = 6 + k, so k = 4. Option A sets k = 10 without subtracting the 6 that the square-root term contributes at Y = 0, while options C and D integrate the square-root term wrongly (forgetting to divide by 1/2, or multiplying by 1/2 instead).

questions.question: In the market penetration model P(t) = M(1 - e^(-kt)), k > 0, where P(t) is the share of a target market that has adopted a new product t months after launch, the constant M represents

options.a: The rate at which the share grows at launch (t = 0)
options.b: The saturation level, the share approached in the long run
options.c: The number of months needed to reach full saturation
options.d: The share of the market that adopts in the first month

questions.explanation: As t grows, e^(-kt) shrinks towards 0, so P(t) rises towards M; M is therefore the saturation level, the largest share the product approaches. Option D describes P(1) = M(1 - e^(-k)), which is smaller than M, and option A describes the initial rate dP/dt at t = 0, which equals Mk. Option C is wrong because M is a share, not a time, and the model never exactly reaches M in finite time.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the graph of P(t) = M(1 - e^(-kt)) for t >= 0, where M > 0 and k > 0?

options.a: It starts at M and falls at a decreasing rate towards 0
options.b: It starts at 0 and rises at an increasing rate without limit
options.c: It starts at 0, rises to a peak of M, then falls back to 0
options.d: It starts at 0 and rises at a decreasing rate towards M

questions.explanation: At t = 0, P = M(1 - 1) = 0, and dP/dt = Mke^(-kt) is positive but shrinking, so the curve rises ever more slowly and levels off towards M. Option A describes the decay curve Me^(-kt), and option B describes unlimited exponential growth. Option C is wrong because P(t) never falls: its derivative is positive for every t.

questions.question: Suppose the proportion of shops in a Lagos market that accept payments through a new POS terminal t months after its launch is P(t) = 0.8(1 - e^(-0.3t)). What percentage of the shops accept it after 4 months? (Correct to 2 decimal places.)
questions.explanation: P(4) = 0.8(1 - e^(-0.3 x 4)) = 0.8(1 - e^(-1.2)) = 0.8(1 - 0.3012) = 0.5590, i.e. 55.90% of the shops. Option D is 0.8e^(-1.2), the part of the saturation share not yet reached, and option B forgets the saturation factor 0.8. Option C multiplies only the exponential term by 0.8, computing 1 - 0.8e^(-1.2).

questions.question: A new video-streaming service has a potential market of 12 million subscribers in Nigeria, and the number of subscribers t months after launch is N(t) = 12(1 - e^(-0.15t)) million. How many subscribers does it have after 6 months? (In millions, correct to 2 decimal places.)
questions.explanation: N(6) = 12(1 - e^(-0.15 x 6)) = 12(1 - e^(-0.9)) = 12(1 - 0.4066) = 7.12 million subscribers. Option C is 12e^(-0.9), the potential subscribers still to join, and option D wrongly treats 1 - e^(-0.9) as 0.9. Option A forgets to multiply by the market size of 12 million.

questions.question: Suppose the number of Lagos households subscribed to a new solar home-power plan t years after launch is N(t) = 50,000(1 - e^(-0.4t)). How many new households subscribe during the third year, that is between t = 2 and t = 3? (To the nearest whole number.)
questions.explanation: New subscribers in the third year are N(3) - N(2) = 50,000(e^(-0.8) - e^(-1.2)) = 50,000(0.44933 - 0.30119) = 7,407 households. Option C is N(3), the total after three years, and option D is N(2), the total after two years. Option A is the average per year over the first three years, N(3)/3, not the number added in the third year.

questions.question: The number of users of a new ride-hailing app in Abuja t months after launch is modelled as N(t) = 4.5 - 4.5e^(-0.3t) million. What number of users does N(t) approach in the long run (as t becomes very large)?
questions.explanation: Rewrite the model as N(t) = 4.5(1 - e^(-0.3t)); as t grows, e^(-0.3t) approaches 0, so N(t) approaches 4.5 million users, the saturation level. Option D adds the two 4.5 terms, option A is 4.5 x 0.3 = 1.35, the initial growth rate in millions per month, and option C divides 4.5 by 0.3.

questions.question: Suppose the share of Lagos supermarkets stocking a new Nigerian-made yoghurt brand t months after launch is P(t) = 0.9(1 - e^(-0.2t)). After how many months will 60% of the supermarkets stock it? (Correct to 2 decimal places.)
questions.explanation: Set 0.9(1 - e^(-0.2t)) = 0.6, so 1 - e^(-0.2t) = 2/3 and e^(-0.2t) = 1/3; then t = ln 3/0.2 = 5.49 months. Option C ignores the saturation level 0.9 and solves e^(-0.2t) = 0.4, and option D solves e^(-0.2t) = 2/3 instead of 1/3. Option B assumes the share keeps growing at its initial rate of 0.9 x 0.2 = 0.18 per month, giving 0.6/0.18.

questions.question: A new mobile savings app's share of its target market t months after launch is P(t) = M(1 - e^(-0.25t)), where M is the saturation level. How long does it take for the share to reach half of M? (Correct to 2 decimal places.)
questions.explanation: Half saturation means M(1 - e^(-0.25t)) = M/2, so e^(-0.25t) = 1/2 and t = ln 2/0.25 = 4 ln 2 = 2.77 months, whatever the value of M. Option D assumes the share grows at its initial rate 0.25M per month, option B uses the common log, 4 log 2 = 1.20, instead of the natural log, and option A multiplies ln 2 by 0.25 instead of dividing.

questions.question: A new Nollywood streaming platform expects its share of Nigerian internet users t years after launch to follow P(t) = 0.8(1 - e^(-kt)). If its share after 5 years is 50%, find k. (Correct to 3 decimal places.)
questions.explanation: From 0.8(1 - e^(-5k)) = 0.5, 1 - e^(-5k) = 0.625, so e^(-5k) = 0.375 and k = -ln(0.375)/5 = 0.196. Option B ignores the saturation level and solves e^(-5k) = 0.5, and option A treats the growth as linear, 0.5/(0.8 x 5). Option C solves e^(-5k) = 0.625, forgetting to subtract from 1.

questions.question: Suppose the proportion of Abuja households using a new LPG cylinder delivery service t years after launch is P(t) = 0.75(1 - e^(-0.5t)). Find the rate of penetration dP/dt when t = 2, in percentage points per year. (Correct to 2 decimal places.)
questions.explanation: dP/dt = 0.75 x 0.5e^(-0.5t) = 0.375e^(-0.5t), so at t = 2 the rate is 0.375e^(-1) = 0.1380, i.e. 13.80 percentage points per year. Option C forgets the factor 0.5 from the chain rule, option D is the share P(2) itself rather than its rate of change, and option A leaves out the saturation level 0.75.

questions.question: The number of Lagos businesses using a new invoicing app t months after launch is modelled by the logistic function N(t) = 50,000/(1 + 24e^(-0.6t)). Find N(5). (To the nearest whole number.)
questions.explanation: N(5) = 50,000/(1 + 24e^(-3)) = 50,000/(1 + 24 x 0.049787) = 50,000/2.1949 = 22,780 businesses. Option B is N(0) = 50,000/25, the number at launch. Option D wrongly adds 1 and 24 before multiplying by e^(-3), and option C is 50,000 - 22,780, the businesses that have not yet adopted.

questions.question: The number of subscribers to a new cable-TV bundle in Ibadan t months after launch is modelled by N(t) = 8,000/(1 + 15e^(-0.4t)). How many subscribers does the bundle have at launch (t = 0)?
questions.explanation: At t = 0, e^0 = 1, so N(0) = 8,000/(1 + 15) = 8,000/16 = 500 subscribers. Option A is the long-run limit as t grows, option D divides 8,000 by 15 and forgets the 1 in the denominator, and option C is 8,000 - 500, the subscribers still to be won.

questions.question: Monthly sales of a new brand of bottled water in Port Harcourt, in thousands of cartons, t months after launch are modelled by N(t) = 360/(1 + 9e^(-0.5t)). What value does N(t) approach as t becomes very large?
questions.explanation: As t becomes very large, e^(-0.5t) approaches 0, so the denominator approaches 1 and N(t) approaches 360 thousand, i.e. 360,000 cartons a month. Option A is the starting value N(0) = 360/10 = 36 thousand, and option C wrongly divides 360 by 9. Option D would follow only if the exponential term grew without bound, which happens for e^(0.5t), not e^(-0.5t).

questions.question: A new machine operator at a bottling plant in Agbara produces Q(t) = 60 - 40e^(-0.2t) crates per hour after t days of training. Find the operator's output after 5 days of training. (Correct to 2 decimal places.)
questions.explanation: Q(5) = 60 - 40e^(-0.2 x 5) = 60 - 40e^(-1) = 60 - 14.72 = 45.28 crates per hour. Option B is only the 40e^(-1) term that should be subtracted, and option D is the starting output Q(0) = 60 - 40. Option A wrongly rewrites the model as 60(1 - e^(-0.2t)), dropping the 40.

questions.question: A trainee tailor at a garment factory in Aba can sew Q(t) = 30 - 25e^(-0.1t) shirts per day after t days on the job. After how many days will the tailor first sew 25 shirts per day? (Correct to 2 decimal places.)
questions.explanation: Set 30 - 25e^(-0.1t) = 25, so 25e^(-0.1t) = 5, e^(-0.1t) = 0.2 and t = ln 5/0.1 = 10 ln 5 = 16.09 days. Option D uses the common log, 10 log 5, instead of ln, and option B multiplies ln 5 by 0.1 instead of dividing. Option C assumes output keeps rising at its starting rate Q'(0) = 25 x 0.1 = 2.5 shirts per day, giving (25 - 5)/2.5 = 8 days.
